nameNote: Mikimiki is a Kāi Tahu form. These names are shared with several other small-leaved shrubs.
summary: A native shrub or small tree with a dense network of spreading branches. It grows in forest, scrub, wetlands and beside streams throughout much of New Zealand.
lookFor: Tiny, narrow dark-green leaves on tangled twigs. Ripe berries are often blue or blue-flecked, although their colour varies.

summary: An evergreen New Zealand tree that often colonises forest edges and disturbed ground. Its small, dark flowers release their scent in the evening.
lookFor: Glossy oval leaves with wavy edges against dark, almost black young stems. Seed capsules split open to reveal sticky black seeds.

summary: A distinctive native tree found across much of New Zealand. Mature trees develop a stout trunk and branching crowns, and can reach about 20 metres.
lookFor: Long, sword-shaped leaves gathered into dense tufts at the ends of branches. Young plants often have one upright stem before branching.

nameNote: Kōwhai is shared by several Sophora species; the botanical name identifies this one.
summary: A native flowering tree known for its hanging yellow flowers. Nectar-feeding birds, including tūī, help pollinate it.
lookFor: Feathery leaves made up of many small leaflets, drooping branches and clusters of yellow flowers. Flowering makes it particularly easy to spot.

summary: One of New Zealand’s largest deciduous native trees. It changes markedly with age: a young plant’s tangled growth develops into a taller tree with larger leaves.
lookFor: Small leaves among interlacing juvenile branches, then larger leaves on older growth. Dense clusters of tiny pale flowers appear in spring.

nameNote: WRT records the name Tawairauriki. Wikipedia also uses the botanical name Nothofagus cliffortioides.
summary: A native beech associated with mountain forests. It can form tall forest, but becomes much shorter and more twisted near the treeline.
lookFor: Small, elongated leaves with pointed tips. Compare the overall tree shape too: exposed mountain trees can look very different from sheltered ones.

summary: A South Island shrub, usually around 2–4 metres tall, with densely interwoven branches. Its small flowers and foliage support native moths and other insects.
lookFor: A twiggy, tangled outline with small pale-green leaves and many small white flowers in spring.

nameNote: NZPCN now lists this plant as Shawia lineata. WRT’s recorded botanical name is retained here.
summary: A fine-leaved native shrub or small tree of southern grey scrub, grassland and forest margins. It often grows around river terraces, seepages and wetland edges.
lookFor: Very narrow leaves with pale, felted undersides and slender drooping branchlets. Small flowers sit on fine stalks.

summary: A tree daisy of the eastern South Island, including Otago and northern Southland. It grows in grey scrub and open rocky country and supports specialist native moths.
lookFor: Opposite pairs of small, dull grey-green leaves, hairy underneath. Fine outer branchlets hang down, and clusters of cream flowers appear in summer.

summary: An evergreen plant that grows in large clumps. Harakeke is an important fibre plant, with a long history of use in Māori weaving.
lookFor: Long, upright strap-like leaves emerging from the base. Tall flowering stalks rise above the foliage with red or yellow flowers.

summary: A hardy native shrub of grassland and forest edges, extending into subalpine areas. Birds disperse the seeds from its small berries.
lookFor: Very reduced, narrow leaves that give the plant a needle-leaved appearance. Purple-white berries can appear in autumn.

nameNote: Toetoe is shared by several native Austroderia species.
summary: A large native tussock grass with flowering stems rising above its leaves. It is one of New Zealand’s toetoe species and is often confused with introduced pampas grasses.
lookFor: Arching, cream to yellowish flower plumes, often drooping to one side. The long leaves have several strong veins as well as a central rib.

summary: A native wetland sedge that thrives with wet roots. Older plants build a raised, trunk-like base from roots and old stems.
lookFor: A fountain of long, narrow, drooping green leaves above a chunky tussock base. Its flower and seed stalks also droop.

nameNote: Mingimingi is shared with other small-leaved shrubs, so it does not uniquely identify this species.
summary: A much-branched native shrub found in scrub, forest and coastal country. Its translucent berries attract birds and skinks.
lookFor: Small, stiff, rounded leaves in opposite pairs, spaced along the branches. They are glossy dark green above and pale underneath.

summary: A native shrub whose many crossing branches create its distinctive wire-netting shape. Yellow flowers are followed by colourful fruit.
lookFor: Grey zigzag twigs, tiny leaves with pale undersides, and small yellow star-shaped flowers when in bloom.

summary: A hardy evergreen native tree with dense foliage. Its small flowers are less conspicuous than its thick, glossy leaves.
lookFor: Broad, leathery yellow-green leaves with smooth edges. The leaf base is often slightly uneven on either side of the stalk.

nameNote: WRT records Mākaka for this plant. It is a shared name for native brooms; a species-specific Māori name has not been confirmed in the sources checked.
summary: An upright native broom with green, largely leafless branchlets. Its small pea-like flowers can be purple, violet and white.
lookFor: An open, stout shrub with green to bronze-green stems. Ripe seed pods droop, a useful feature for distinguishing it from other native brooms.

summary: A native conifer especially associated with mountain forests. Older references may call it Podocarpus hallii or Podocarpus cunninghamii.
lookFor: Narrow, pointed leaves and thin, papery bark that flakes away. Its bark is thinner than that of lowland tōtara, and juvenile leaves are longer.

nameNote: Mikimiki is a shared name used for several small-leaved Coprosma species.
summary: A small-leaved native shrub or tree with tangled, slender branches. It occurs in eastern and southern parts of New Zealand.
lookFor: Tiny leaves with wavy edges or blunt teeth. The pale, translucent ripe berries can look green because the seeds show through.

summary: A deciduous native tree daisy with reddish young stems and furrowed bark. It supports many native moth species and needs open ground for seedlings to establish.
lookFor: Clusters of grey-green leaves arranged opposite one another, with silvery undersides. Its small flower heads contain pale-yellow florets.
